title: The sick first (ch. 36)
hook: care of the sick is placed above all

segments.voice: Yesterday, tools as altar vessels: the saucepan handled like the chalice. Your line was everything is holy. Which tool did you clean and put back? Day one thousand two hundred one.

Before all things, and above all things. Strong words for any rule to use, and Saint Benedict doesn't spend them lightly. Earlier this week the Rule said nothing is to be put before the work of God, the hours of prayer. So what could possibly come before all things? Not the abbot. Not the chapel. Not the harvest or the library. Chapter thirty-six answers in its first line, and the answer is the brother lying in the infirmary with a fever. Today: the sick first.
screen: `BEFORE ALL THINGS, ABOVE ALL THINGS.` → `WHAT COULD COME BEFORE EVERYTHING?` → `THE BROTHER WITH A FEVER.`

segments.voice: Benedict writes that care of the sick must come before all things and above all things, so that they are served as Christ himself. And he gives Christ's words from Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "sick, and you visited me," and "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." One way to hold the two "before" lines together: the work of God comes first, and the sick are served as Christ. It's the same Christ, in the chapel and in the sickbed. Then Benedict gets specific. The sick get their own room, and a brother to look after them who is God-fearing, careful and attentive. They may have baths as often as it helps them. The very weak may eat meat, normally kept off the monks' table, to get their strength back; when they recover, they go back to the usual fare. The abbot is to take the greatest care that the sick suffer no neglect, and to check that the cellarer and the attendants don't let anything slip. And here's the part that keeps it honest. Benedict speaks to the sick, too. They should remember they're being served for the honor of God, and not wear out their brothers with unreasonable demands. And then, in the very next breath, he tells the brothers: bear with them patiently anyway, because from such as these a greater reward is gained. Patience is asked of both sides of the bed. Nobody in this chapter is a saint already. They're just people being asked to carry each other.
screen: `THE SICK: BEFORE ALL, ABOVE ALL.` · `SERVED AS CHRIST HIMSELF.` · `A ROOM, A CAREFUL NURSE, BATHS, MEAT.` · `PATIENCE ON BOTH SIDES OF THE BED.` · then, large: `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit someone ill, and start the visit here. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is sick right now. In the hospital, at home with a long illness, worn down by something nobody sees. Hold their face in your mind for a few breaths. Then decide on one real step you can take today: a visit if you can, a call, a message, a meal left at the door. Make it concrete: when, and how. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just keep them in mind a little longer, kindly. The bell holds the time.
The sick first. In Benedict's Rule, care of the sick comes before all things and above all things, because they are served as Christ. Today's word.
Your line: before all things. Today, take the one step you chose toward someone who is ill, before the rest of your list, not after it. Day one thousand two hundred one.

howItsDone: Benedictine communities care for their sick and elderly members within the monastery, and Catholics count visiting the sick among the corporal works of mercy drawn from Matthew 25.

fork.setup: you're nursing a sick brother who keeps asking for more than seems reasonable. what does chapter thirty-six ask of you?
options: tell him firmly that he's asking too much.
bear with him patiently: from such as these a greater reward is gained.
ask the abbot to move him somewhere else.
fork.reveal: Benedict asks the sick not to make excessive demands, and still asks the brothers to bear with them patiently.

original.note: Latin, from the first line of chapter thirty-six: before all things and above all things.

trapdoor: what you thought: be kind to people who are sick.
what it means: in Benedict's house, care of the sick comes before all things, because the sick are served as Christ.
what a scholar hears: the chapter rests on Matthew 25:36 and 25:40 and asks patience of both sides: no excess demands, and patient bearing anyway.

notes: Editor pass: the reconciliation of chapter 36 with chapter 43 is now offered as one way to read them, not as the narrator's ruling.

The Rule is paraphrased. Check the summary of ch. 36: 'Infirmorum cura ante omnia et super omnia adhibenda est', served as Christ; Matthew 25:36 and 25:40; the sick not to distress the brothers by superfluous demands, yet to be borne patiently, since from such a greater reward is gained; the abbot's great care that they suffer no neglect; a separate cell and a God-fearing, diligent, careful attendant; baths as often as expedient; meat for the very weak, given up on recovery; the abbot to see that cellarer and attendants do not neglect them.

The reconciliation of ch. 36 ('before all things') with ch. 43 ('nothing before the work of God') as 'the same Christ, in the chapel and in the sickbed' is the script's own reading, not the Rule's; confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
'meat, normally kept off the monks' table' refers to the Rule's restriction on the flesh of four-footed animals (ch. 39); confirm the simplified phrasing.
howItsDone: visiting the sick as one of the corporal works of mercy; confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Matthew 25:36 and 25:40.
